name: BQ21040DBVR
title: bq21040: 0.8 A single-input linear charger for one Li-Ion or Li-Pol cell, SOT-23
summary: A linear charger for one Li-Ion or Li-Pol cell in a six-pin SOT-23, with its pass FET and current sense inside. It runs from USB or an adapter, takes up to 30 V on IN and stops charging above about 6.6 V. It charges in three stages (pre-charge, then constant current, then constant voltage) to 4.2 V with 1% accuracy; a resistor on ISET sets fast charge up to 800 mA, with pre-charge fixed at 20% and the done threshold at 10% of it. Protection covers input DPM, thermal regulation at 125 °C, shorted OUT or ISET, NTC battery temperature and a 10-hour safety timer; an open-drain CHG pin shows charging.
key_figures: 30 V abs max; OVP 6.65 V typ

notes: The four orderable numbers differ in reel quantity: 3000 or 250 pieces.

pins.name: TS
pins.function: Battery temperature input for the pack's 10 kΩ-at-25 °C NTC, which the part biases from an internal current source. Left open or pulled high it puts the part in TTDM, turning off TS monitoring, the timers and termination; held low it disables the charger. Without a thermistor, a fixed 10 kΩ to VSS gives normal operation. Adding 237 kΩ between TS and ground keeps the part out of TTDM when a pack with its thermistor is taken away.

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Charger output to the battery; a system load may share it. Bypass with 1 µF to 10 µF.

pins.name: CHG
pins.function: Open-drain status. The FET is on (pin low) while charging and off (open) when not charging or once charging has finished.

pins.name: ISET
pins.function: Fast-charge current setting: a resistor to VSS sets the current, from 10.8 kΩ for 50 mA down to 675 Ω for 800 mA.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input from a DC source such as an AC adapter or a USB port. Bypass to VSS with 1 µF to 10 µF.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: A single Li-Ion or Li-Pol cell charged from a 5 V source at 540 mA fast charge, which puts pre-charge at 108 mA and the CHG threshold at 54 mA. RISET (1.0 kΩ, from KISET = 540 AΩ) sets the fast-charge current. The pack's 10 kΩ NTC (103AT) goes from TS to the pack's negative terminal at ground. An LED with RCHG in series runs from OUT into the open-drain CHG pin to show charging. A 1 µF ceramic sits on VIN and another on OUT, where a system load may hang beside the battery.
notes: For a host instead of an LED, a pull-up from the host's supply rail to CHG reads the status.

where.KISET: fast charge current factor, 540 AΩ typical above 60 mA

where.t: time to drain a full battery

equations.note: 0.75 Ah at 10 µA gives 75 000 h, about 8.8 years.

operation.text: A linear charger for one Li-Ion or Li-Pol cell with its pass FET and current sense inside, fed from USB or an adapter and rated to 30 V at IN with overvoltage cut-off at about 6.6 V. Charging runs in three phases: pre-charge for a deeply flat cell, constant current, then constant voltage at 4.2 V. Pre-charge is fixed at 20% and the CHG threshold at 10% of the fast-charge current, which one resistor on ISET sets up to 800 mA. There is one output; a system load may sit across the battery so long as its average draw still lets the battery fill within the 10-hour safety timer.

Below VLOWV (2.5 V) the cell gets pre-charge current. Above it the fast-charge current set on ISET flows; dissipation in the part peaks in this phase while the battery voltage is low. When the cell reaches regulation voltage the voltage loop holds it there while the current falls to the termination level. Before charging starts on a 5 V source the part tests ISET and OUT for shorts.

At a junction temperature of 125 °C the part lowers the charge current as far as needed to stop the temperature rising and runs its timer clock at half speed. Thermal shutdown is at 155 °C typical with 20 °C hysteresis. Designs should not sit in thermal regulation under nominal input and ambient; the loop still works if it is always active.
With IN under the UVLO threshold the part is off and every pin is high impedance. Rising past UVLO it enters sleep or active operation according to the battery voltage at OUT.

Past UVLO the part resets its logic and timers and starts monitoring. Once power is good (VBAT + VDT < VIN < VOVP and above UVLO) and TS is above the enable threshold, it charges at a 100 mA limit, runs the ISET and OUT short tests, starts the safety timer and turns on CHG, then moves to the current set on ISET.

With IN between UVLO and VOUT + VDT, charging stops, the safety timer pauses without resetting and CHG goes high impedance. When IN rises again the timer resumes, charging restarts and CHG returns to its earlier state.

A charge cycle starts on applying good power, on a disable and re-enable through TS, on leaving TTDM, on a battery being inserted, or when OUT falls below VRCH. CHG goes low only in the first cycle; leaving TTDM or falling below VRCH does not turn it back on if it is already off.

Monitored all the time. An overvoltage turns the pass FET off after a blanking time, stops the timer and puts CHG high impedance. When IN returns to normal the timer and charging resume and CHG goes low after a 25 ms deglitch.

The open-drain FET is on only during the first charge, whether or not in TTDM, and turns off once the battery is in voltage regulation and the current has fallen to 10% of the programmed value. It goes high impedance during sleep or OVP, then resumes its previous state. Cycling input power, pulling TS low and releasing it, or entering pre-charge resets it and counts as a first charge. For a host, pull it up to the host supply; for a lamp, use a resistor and LED to a supply. If that supply can exceed 7 V, clamp the pin with a 6.2 V Zener. An LED fed from OUT changes brightness with battery voltage.

When the source sags to VIN-DPM (4.3 V typical) because it is at its current limit, the pass FET cuts current until IN stops falling, so a source below VIN-DPM cannot drive OUT. This suits current-limited adapters and USB ports whose nominal voltage is above 4.3 V.

OUT feeds the battery and any system load: the part can charge and supply together, charge only, or only supply the system in TTDM, within the available current. OUT is current limited and so short protected. A load above the programmed current discharges the output unless a charged battery or enough capacitance makes up the difference.

The resistor sets 50 mA to 800 mA and can also serve as a current monitor. At low current the part disables a section of its sense FET for better resolution; going from high to low current there is hysteresis and the change happens near 0.15 A. The pin detects a resistance below about 340 Ω when at least 80 mA flows and then latches the charger off until power is cycled. Separately, OUT current is clamped between 1.05 A and 1.4 A.

TS follows the Li-Ion temperature standard with thresholds at 0 °C and 45 °C; charging runs between them and stops outside. A 50 µA internal source biases a 10 kΩ NTC with β = 3370 (SEMITEC 103AT-2 or Mitsubishi TH05-3H103F) from TS to VSS. Because the current and thresholds are fixed, only a 10 kΩ (at 25 °C) NTC works. Without the feature, a fixed 10 kΩ to VSS lets the part run normally, for instance with a host watching the thermistor and pulling TS low to stop charge. Pulled low, TS disables charging and its current drops to about 30 µA; floated or driven high it selects TTDM. From about –10 °C down to –50 °C the bias current is cut back so that a cold thermistor does not trip TTDM.

TS going high, by removing a pack with its thermistor or pulling TS to the TTDM threshold, enters termination and timer disable mode: the 10-hour timer stays reset and termination stops, while the charge stages themselves are unchanged and current tapers to zero. A battery detect runs on entry; with no battery CHG goes high impedance, otherwise CHG changes only when current reaches the termination level, and the output stays regulated. On leaving TTDM, battery detect runs and a found battery starts a new cycle with the LED on. A 237 kΩ from TS to VSS stops a removed pack from putting the part in TTDM, at the cost of about 0.1 °C error hot and 3 °C cold.

Pre-charge is limited to 30 minutes and fast charge to 10 hours. Thermal regulation, input DPM or a USB current limit halves the timer clock and so stretches the time. When either timer expires charging ends and CHG goes high impedance. Disabling the part, cycling power or passing through TTDM resets the fast-charge timer.

With OUT above VRCH and current down to 10% of fast charge, CHG goes high impedance and battery detect runs. A battery still present ends charging. A battery removed with its thermistor lets TS rise into TTDM; a battery removed while TS stays in its active range keeps battery detect running until one is inserted.

Runs on entering and leaving TTDM, all the time while no battery is present outside TTDM, and at power-up when the battery is above VRCH; it is off in TTDM and during a TS fault. It waits 25 ms: if OUT is below VREG – 100 mV a battery is present. Otherwise it drops regulation to VREG – 400 mV, turns on a sink current and waits 25 ms more: OUT above VREG – 300 mV means a battery is there; if not, the battery is absent, charge is not signalled and the sink turns off. CHG stays high impedance with no battery.
After termination, OUT falling to VRCH (100 mV under regulation) starts a new charge with CHG left off.

During a cycle's first minute the part lifts the termination level by about 14%, so a full battery re-inserted ends charging in under a minute. A cell rested for many hours may need several minutes before its current falls to termination.

A ceramic decoupling capacitor on IN and on OUT is usually all that is needed; 1 µF each is the typical value, with 1 µF to 10 µF the range on both pins. Smaller values can suit DC loads and larger ones fast, large pulsed loads. Rate the IN capacitor for the highest voltage a bad adapter can apply; ceramic capacitors are tested at twice rating, so a 16 V part may do for a 30 V transient if its maker confirms the test rating.
The source should give 3.5 V to 28 V and at least the highest charge current, well regulated. A source more than a few inches from IN and GND calls for a larger capacitor.

Put the IN and OUT capacitors as close to the part as possible with short traces to IN, OUT and GND. Keep low-current ground returns apart from the battery's high-current paths and join them at one point. Size the IN and OUT traces for the full charge current. Tie the ground connection to the PCB ground with several 10 mil vias near the part to carry heat to a bottom ground plane, and keep traces from cutting that plane under it. A thinner board runs cooler; the EVM is 0.031 in thick with 2 oz copper on both sides.

Dissipation peaks at the start of charge when the battery is lowest. Pack voltage usually reaches about 3.4 V within two minutes of fast charge, faster than the assembly heats, so 3.4 V is a fair minimum battery voltage for worst-case dissipation. Check it with a flat battery by logging board temperature under the part, charge current and battery voltage over time; the current falls off if thermal regulation starts. Board mounting, trace size and copper, orientation, surrounding air and airflow, and nearby surfaces all change the measured ψJT.
Battery current into OUT with no input is 1 µA maximum. Even a 10 µA leak would drain 0.75 Ah in 75 000 hours, far slower than the cell's own self-discharge.
